clinicalPearls: Neuroendocrine tumour of extra-adrenal paraganglia; sympathetic (thoracic, abdominal, pelvic) tumours are often catecholamine-secreting, whereas parasympathetic (head and neck) tumours are usually non-secretory

Head and neck paragangliomas (carotid body, jugulotympanic, vagal) typically present as slowly growing painless masses with cranial nerve palsies or pulsatile tinnitus rather than catecholamine excess
Functional tumours cause paroxysmal or sustained hypertension, headache, palpitations and sweating, mirroring phaeochromocytoma

Up to 40 per cent are hereditary; germline succinate dehydrogenase (SDHB, SDHD, SDHC and related) mutations are commonest, so genetic testing and counselling are recommended in essentially all patients
SDHB mutations carry a notably higher risk of malignant (metastatic) disease and of extra-adrenal, abdominal tumours
Biochemical screening with plasma free or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines is essential before any intervention; some tumours secrete predominantly noradrenaline or dopamine
Somatostatin receptor PET (DOTATATE) is highly sensitive, particularly for SDHB-related and metastatic disease, complementing MIBG and cross-sectional imaging
Preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade, established before any beta-blockade, is mandatory for secretory tumours to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis
reference.pathophysiology: Paragangliomas arise from neural crest-derived chromaffin or glomus cells of the autonomic paraganglia. Sympathetic paraganglia along the paravertebral and para-aortic chains may synthesise and release catecholamines, producing the adrenergic syndrome, whereas parasympathetic paraganglia of the head and neck rarely secrete and instead cause symptoms through local mass effect. A large fraction are driven by germline mutations, most often in the succinate dehydrogenase complex genes; loss of SDH function causes succinate accumulation and a pseudohypoxic state that stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors and promotes tumorigenesis. Malignancy is defined by the presence of metastases at sites where paraganglia are not normally found.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of paroxysmal symptoms and secondary hypertension (anxiety or panic, thyrotoxicosis)
Head and neck schwannoma, nodal mass or carotid aneurysm mimicking a carotid body tumour
Metastatic neuroendocrine tumour from another primary
Medullary thyroid carcinoma within a hereditary syndrome
Neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroma in younger patients
additionalInvestigations: Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines
Plasma or urinary methoxytyramine where a dopamine-secreting tumour is suspected
Contrast CT or MRI of the relevant region (neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis)
Somatostatin receptor PET/CT (DOTATATE), with MIBG scintigraphy in selected cases
Germline genetic testing (SDHx and extended panel) with genetic counselling
SDHB immunohistochemistry on resected tissue to guide genetic evaluation
Whole-body imaging for multifocal or metastatic disease, especially in SDHB carriers
redFlags: Hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia or catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy
Rapid tumour growth, local invasion or metastatic disease (SDHB association)
New cranial neuropathies from an enlarging skull-base or neck tumour
Symptoms provoked by anaesthesia, biopsy or tumour manipulation without prior blockade
Family history of paraganglioma or phaeochromocytoma indicating a hereditary syndrome
reference.prognosis: Benign, completely resected paragangliomas have an excellent prognosis, but metastatic disease, which is more frequent with SDHB mutations, reduces survival although its course can still be prolonged; lifelong surveillance is required because of multifocal and recurrent disease.
pitfalls: Biopsying or operating on a secretory tumour without excluding catecholamine excess and without alpha-blockade, precipitating a hypertensive crisis
Giving beta-blockade before adequate alpha-blockade, causing unopposed alpha vasoconstriction
Assuming head and neck paragangliomas are always non-secretory and omitting biochemical screening
Not offering germline genetic testing, thereby missing hereditary and malignancy risk
Relying on histology alone to predict malignancy, which is defined by the presence of metastasis
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma
WHO Classification of Tumours: Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: Complete surgical resection is the definitive treatment for localised paraganglioma

For catecholamine-secreting tumours, preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin followed by beta-blockade, together with volume expansion, before any surgery or intervention
Systemic treatment of metastatic disease with radionuclide therapy such as I-131 MIBG or lutetium-177 DOTATATE peptide receptor therapy, cytotoxic chemotherapy or external-beam radiotherapy
Germline genetic testing across the SDHx and extended panel with genetic counselling, recommended in essentially all patients
Lifelong biochemical and imaging surveillance for multifocal, recurrent and metastatic disease, particularly with SDHB mutations
Cascade genetic testing and screening of at-risk relatives
Management within an endocrine and endocrine-surgery multidisciplinary team
